summary: This document describes a way to negotiate encrypt-then-MAC in TLS and DTLS in place of the existing MAC-then-encrypt approach. The older ordering has been the subject of several security vulnerabilities over the years.

plainLanguage.summary: There are two ways to seal a secret note: sign it then lock it, or lock it then sign it. This RFC lets two computers agree to use the safer order.

questions: why is mac then encrypt insecure
subtitle: A TLS and DTLS extension that lets both sides switch to the safer order of encrypting first and adding the MAC afterwards.

tldr.problem: TLS and DTLS compute the MAC first and then encrypt it together with the data. That construction is no longer regarded as secure and has been the subject of numerous attacks over many years.
tldr.mechanism: A new empty extension, encrypt_then_mac, lets client and server agree to encrypt the data and padding first and then append a MAC computed over the ciphertext.
tldr.outcome: Both sides can upgrade to the safer ordering without defining new ciphersuites, though it applies only to block ciphers and cannot be used with SSL 3.0.

facts.label: Applies to
facts.value: Block ciphers only, not stream or AEAD

today: RFC 7366 is a Proposed Standard from September 2014 and, per the metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated.

sections.title: Why MAC-then-Encrypt Is a Problem
sections.content:
TLS and DTLS use a MAC-then-encrypt construction. It was regarded as secure when the original SSL protocol was specified in the mid-1990s, but it is no longer regarded as secure. It has been the subject of numerous security vulnerabilities and attacks over a period of many years.

This document specifies a way to switch to the encrypt-then-MAC construction during the TLS/DTLS handshake. Here MAC means Message Authentication Code, a short value that lets the receiver check that data was not altered.
sections.plainLanguage: The old way of sealing a message has turned out to have weak spots. This RFC lets computers use a better way.

sections.title: Negotiating Encrypt-then-MAC
sections.content:
The client includes an encrypt_then_mac extension in its client_hello if it wants encrypt-then-MAC instead of the default. If the server can do it, it answers with encrypt_then_mac in its server_hello. The extension_type value is 22 (0x16) and the extension_data field is empty.

Both sides MUST NOT use encrypt-then-MAC unless both have successfully exchanged the extension.

Using an extension rather than new ciphersuites avoids a Cartesian explosion of suites, since every existing suite would otherwise need a duplicate. The RFC also notes that extensions rule out SSL 3.0, which it considers not worth accommodating.
sections.plainLanguage: The client asks, 'Can we use the safer way?' and the server says 'Yes' by saying the same magic word back. If only one of them says it, they keep the old way.

sections.title: How Records Change
sections.content:
Once negotiated, packet processing changes from encrypt( data || MAC || pad ) to encrypt( data || pad ) || MAC. The MAC covers the whole packet up to the start of the MAC value, so it is now computed over the ciphertext rather than the plaintext.

For TLS 1.1 and greater the MAC input is the sequence number, record type, version, length, the explicit IV and the encrypted content with its padding. For TLS 1.0 without an explicit IV the IV is left out. In DTLS the sequence number is replaced by the combined epoch and sequence number.

The record layout is otherwise unchanged: the MAC value simply moves outside the encrypted data.
sections.plainLanguage: Before, the signature was tucked inside the locked box. Now the box is locked first and the signature is stuck on the outside.

sections.title: Processing Rules and Scope
sections.content:
On receipt, the MAC SHALL be evaluated before any further processing such as decryption, and if verification fails, processing SHALL terminate immediately. For TLS a fatal bad_record_mac MUST be generated. For DTLS the record MUST be discarded and a fatal bad_record_mac MAY be generated. The RFC says this immediate response eliminates timing channels available through manipulated packet data.

The change applies only to standard block ciphers with distinct encrypt and MAC operations. It does not apply to stream ciphers or to AEAD ciphersuites, which already include integrity protection. If a server gets the extension from a client and then selects a stream or AEAD ciphersuite, it MUST NOT send the extension back.

Implementations may negotiate a truncated MAC through the truncated_hmac extension.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver checks the signature first and stops right away if it looks wrong, without opening the box. Some boxes already have a built-in seal, so they do not need this.

sections.title: Rehandshakes
sections.content:
The setting can change during a rehandshake. Implementations SHOULD keep the current session's mechanism across all rehandshakes and SHOULD NOT change it. If they want to be more flexible, the rules are: MAC-then-encrypt to MAC-then-encrypt is no change; MAC-then-encrypt to encrypt-then-MAC is an upgrade; encrypt-then-MAC to encrypt-then-MAC is no change; and encrypt-then-MAC to MAC-then-encrypt is an error.

Implementations MUST NOT renegotiate a downgrade from encrypt-then-MAC to MAC-then-encrypt. This includes a downgrade that happens indirectly through an AEAD ciphersuite in between. An upgrade takes effect in the first message after the Change Cipher Spec message.
sections.plainLanguage: Once you have switched to the safer way, you are not allowed to switch back to the old way, even in a roundabout path.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Encrypt-then-MAC is regarded as more secure and should mitigate or eliminate a number of attacks on the current mechanism, provided the MAC processing instructions are followed.

An active attacker who can emulate a client or server that does not tolerate extensions may cause some implementations to fall back to older protocol versions without extensions, which forces non-encrypt-then-MAC behaviour. The straightforward solution is to avoid fallback to older, less secure versions. IANA has added extension code point 22 (0x16) for encrypt_then_mac to the TLS ExtensionType Values registry.
sections.plainLanguage: A sneaky attacker might trick the computers into the old way by pretending not to understand the new one. The best defence is to refuse to go back to old versions.
